title: Accelerating the Grokking Transition
question: Design the training rule -- update, training loss and metered use of the training data -- that brings generalisation forward on grokking problems whose delay has different causes.
elab:
A network can memorize its training set long before it generalizes; the task develops training rules that shorten this delay on norm-driven MNIST grokking and on standard-initialisation modular-arithmetic grokking with transformers and MLPs.

A network trained on a small training set can fit it almost immediately and then sit near chance on held-out data for a very long time before generalisation appears. Which training rule, given the parameters, the gradients and a metered handle on the training data, removes that delay? The delay has different causes in different settings: an inflated initial weight norm on MNIST, and softmax collapse or slow circuit formation on modular arithmetic at standard initialisation. Norm projection, slow-gradient amplification, perpendicular gradients, spectral whitening, Muon and meta-learned gradient transforms each win somewhere and fail elsewhere. The task measures the rule on six settings across MLPs and transformers. It matters because the delay is a clean, reproducible instance of the gap between memorisation and generalisation, and a rule that closes it everywhere would say something about what generalisation needs.

description_md:
# Removing the delay between memorisation and generalisation

## Research Question

A network trained on a small training set can fit it almost immediately and then sit
near chance on held-out data for a very long time before generalisation finally appears
("grokking"). **What training rule -- the update, the training loss it differentiates,
and any extra use it makes of the training data, all charged against the same budget
of training passes -- removes that delay, across networks and tasks whose delay has
different causes?**

## Background

Power, Burda, Edwards, Babuschkin and Misra (*Grokking: Generalization Beyond Overfitting
on Small Algorithmic Datasets*, arXiv:2201.02177) named the phenomenon on modular
arithmetic. Nanda, Chan, Lieberum, Smith and Steinhardt (*Progress Measures for Grokking
via Mechanistic Interpretability*, ICLR 2023, arXiv:2301.05217) reverse-engineered the
circuit a one-layer transformer forms for modular addition and showed that the
generalising circuit forms gradually long before test accuracy moves. Liu, Michaud and
Tegmark (*Omnigrok: Grokking Beyond Algorithmic Data*, ICLR 2023, arXiv:2210.01117)
explain part of it by weight norm: on the sphere of a given norm the test loss has a
"Goldilocks zone", so a network initialised far outside it fits first and generalises
only once something carries the norm back in. Not every delay is of that kind: Prieto,
Barsbey, Mediano and Birdal (*Grokking at the Edge of Numerical Stability*, ICLR 2025,
arXiv:2501.04697) trace the delay at standard initialisation to the gradient aligning
with the "naive loss minimisation" direction that scales the logits up until the
softmax collapses numerically. Lee, Kang, Kim and Lee (*Grokfast*, arXiv:2405.20233)
treat the gradient sequence as a signal and amplify its slow component; Pasand and
Dohmatob (*Egalitarian Gradient Descent*, ICLR 2026, arXiv:2510.04930) equalise the
speed of every principal direction of the gradient; Tveit, Remseth and Skogvold
(arXiv:2504.16041) report that the Muon optimiser alone shortens the delay; Zhou, Fan,
Jaggi and Fu (*NeuralGrok*, arXiv:2504.17243) meta-learn a gradient transformation on a
held-back slice of the training data. Decoupled weight decay is Loshchilov and Hutter
(ICLR 2019, arXiv:1711.05101).

The rule is scored on several training problems: ReLU MLPs and transformers, trained
with MSE and with cross-entropy, full-batch and mini-batch, from inflated and from
standard initialisations. A rule
that fixes only the weight norm, or only the logit scale, does not by itself settle all
of them.

## What You Can Modify

`Omnigrok/custom_rule.py`, the editable region only:

```python
class UpdateRule:
    def __init__(self, model, setting, budget, benchmark, trainer): ...
    def loss(self, outputs, targets, indices): ...
    def step(self, model, step_index): ...
```

`__init__` is called once before training, with the model, an opaque evaluation-setting
label (stable across runs, so a rule may specialise per setting, but carrying nothing
about the setting itself), the step budget, `benchmark` -- the network family the
setting uses: `"mnist"` (a ReLU MLP whose default loss is MSE on one-hot labels),
`"modadd-transformer"` (a one-layer transformer), `"modadd-mlp"` (a two-hidden-layer
ReLU MLP) or `"modarith-decoder"` (a two-layer causal transformer decoder), the last three
with cross-entropy as default loss -- and `trainer`, a metered handle on the training
set: `trainer.n_train`, `trainer.batch_size` (examples per step),
`trainer.batch_indices` (the current step's batch), `trainer.charged`, and
`trainer.loss_at(indices, params=None, loss_fn=None)`, which returns the differentiable
training loss on the training examples `indices`, at the current parameters or at
`params` (a name -> tensor mapping), with the rule's own `loss` or `loss_fn`.

Each step the driver evaluates the model on the step's batch, calls
`loss(outputs, targets, indices)` (`targets` are class labels, `indices` the batch's
positions in the training set; `default_loss(benchmark, outputs, targets)` is each
benchmark's own loss; on `"mnist"` the MSE loss is fixed and `loss` is not consulted),
back-propagates it, and calls `step`, which must update the
parameters **in place** and return nothing. State of your own -- momenta, filters,
auxiliary networks -- may live on the rule object.

**The budget counts training passes.** Each driver step is one pass over its batch, and
every `trainer.loss_at` call is charged `len(indices) / trainer.batch_size` passes on top;
held-out accuracy is checkpointed on a fixed grid of passes spent.

The parameter set and every tensor shape of the model must be unchanged: each checkpoint
is reloaded into a freshly built model with `strict=True`, so adding, removing or
reshaping a parameter of `model` produces no result at all. Auxiliary trainable
parameters a rule's optimisers hold are capped (see the parameter budget). Only `torch`
and the standard library are available. A rule whose construction, `loss` or `step`
raises produces no result.

## Fixed by the Harness

Everything else is fixed by the harness: the training data and its size, the networks,
their initialisation, the batch stream, the budget of training passes and the
checkpoint grid. The rule runs in its own process, which is given its training data and nothing
else -- no path to any held-out data and, where the container permits it, no privilege
to read it. The metric is computed afterwards by a separate fixed process from the
checkpoints that process wrote. The held-out data it scores against is not in your
workspace image; it is available only for the final evaluation.

## Reference Baselines

```python
# adam_nowd -- Adam, no weight decay (betas (0.9, 0.98) on the modular families)
torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3, weight_decay=0.0)

# adamw -- decoupled weight decay at each benchmark's published default
#   (Loshchilov & Hutter, ICLR 2019; Omnigrok's MNIST notebook: wd 0.01;
#    Power et al. / Nanda et al. on modular arithmetic: wd 1.0, betas (0.9, 0.98))
torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3, weight_decay=wd)

# sphere_fixed -- Omnigrok's fixed-weight-norm procedure: Adam, then hold the total
#   norm at the value the network starts from
scale = ||theta_init|| / ||theta||

# goldilocks_project -- Omnigrok's cure: constrain the norm to the Goldilocks sphere
#   (the alpha = 1 initialisation radius on MNIST; 0.8 x the standard-initialisation
#    norm with AdamW(wd 0, betas (0.9, 0.98)) on modular addition, as in their notebook)
scale = target_radius / ||theta||

# grokfast_ema -- amplify the low-pass-filtered gradient (ironjr/grokfast gradfilter_ema)
state[n] = state[n] * alpha + p.grad * (1 - alpha)
p.grad   = p.grad + state[n] * lamb
#   MNIST: alpha 0.8, lamb 0.1, AdamW(wd 2.0); algorithmic: alpha 0.98, lamb 2.0,
#   Adam(wd 0.005, betas (0.9, 0.98)), 10-step warm-up

# grokfast_ma -- the same idea with a sliding-window mean (gradfilter_ma)
p.grad = p.grad + mean(last 100 grads) * 5.0    # MNIST AdamW(wd 0.01); algorithmic Adam(wd 0.01)

# ortho_adamw -- ⊥AdamW (Prieto et al., ICLR 2025, orthograd.OrthoGrad): remove the
#   gradient component along the weights, restore the gradient norm, then AdamW
#   (betas (0.9, 0.999), eps 1e-8, wd 0; lr 5e-3 on the modular MLP, 1e-3 elsewhere)
g_orth = g - (w.g / w.w) w ;  g <- g_orth * ||g|| / ||g_orth||

# egd -- Egalitarian Gradient Descent (Pasand & Dohmatob, ICLR 2026): whiten each
#   selected weight-matrix gradient, G = U S V^T  ->  U V^T, then the base optimiser
#   (MLPs: every Linear weight, AdamW(wd 0.01); transformers: MLP weights,
#    Adam(wd 0.005, betas (0.9, 0.98)), 10-step warm-up)

# neuralgrok -- NeuralGrok (Zhou et al., arXiv:2504.17243, Blackzxy/NeuralOptGrok):
#   an amplifier MLP (1-128-128-1, softmax over each tensor's entries) rescales every
#   gradient, g <- 0.2 * p(g) * g / ||p(g) * g||, clip 1.0, Adam(wd 1e-3); every 4 steps
#   the amplifier is updated on the loss of a held-back 2% of the training set after a
#   simulated step (bilevel), via trainer.loss_at
#
# stablemax -- StableMax cross-entropy (Prieto et al.): s(x) = x + 1 (x >= 0),
#   1 / (1 - x) (x < 0) in place of exp, float64; AdamW(lr 0.01, betas (0.9, 0.999))
#
# muon -- Muon (Tveit et al., arXiv:2504.16041; reference KellerJordan/Muon):
#   Newton-Schulz-orthogonalised Nesterov momentum (lr 0.02, momentum 0.95) on hidden
#   weight matrices, the benchmark's AdamW on embeddings, input/output layers and vectors
```

## Metric

**log10 of the generalisation step**: the base-10 logarithm of the first *checkpoint* --
on a fixed log-spaced grid of 12 points per decade of training passes spent, the same
grid for every submission -- at which held-out accuracy reaches the setting's threshold,
censored at the budget.
**Lower is better.** (The grid is why this is a checkpoint index rather than an exact
step: held-out accuracy is measured only at those checkpoints, by a separate process.)
Held-out accuracy at the end of the run, the best value it reached, the step at which
the training set was memorised and the final weight norm are reported alongside it but
are not scored. Settings are combined into a single task score.

_FILE = "Omnigrok/custom_rule.py"

_CONTENT = '''class UpdateRule:
    """Adam, learning rate 1e-3, no weight decay."""

    def __init__(self, model, setting, budget, benchmark, trainer):
        self.benchmark = benchmark
        betas = (0.9, 0.999) if benchmark == "mnist" else (0.9, 0.98)
        self.opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3, betas=betas, weight_decay=0.0)
        self.sched = None
        if benchmark == "modarith-decoder":   # grokfast main.py: 10-update linear warm-up
            self.sched = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.LambdaLR(
                self.opt, lambda update: 1 if update > 10 else update / 10)

    def loss(self, outputs, targets, indices):
        return default_loss(self.benchmark, outputs, targets)

    def step(self, model, step_index):
        self.opt.step()
        if self.sched is not None:
            self.sched.step()
'''

"""The optimisation / regularisation rule for the grokking experiments.

The FIXED driver (`Omnigrok/mlsb_stage2_train.py`) owns everything except this file:
the training data, the network, its initialisation, the loss, the batch stream, the
step budget and the checkpoint grid. Once per optimisation step it

    1. computes `UpdateRule.loss` on the step's training batch,
    2. calls `model.zero_grad()` and `loss.backward()`, so that `p.grad` is populated
       for every parameter of `model`,
    3. calls `UpdateRule.step(model, step_index)`,

and saves `model.state_dict()` at each point of the checkpoint grid. A separate fixed
process loads those checkpoints afterwards and scores them.

CONTRACT
--------
* `UpdateRule.__init__(model, setting, budget, benchmark, trainer)` is called once,
  before training. `setting` is an opaque, stable label of the evaluation setting,
  `budget` the step budget, and `benchmark` the network family the setting uses -- one of

      "mnist"               a ReLU MLP, default loss MSE on one-hot labels,
      "modadd-transformer"  a one-layer transformer, default loss cross-entropy,
      "modadd-mlp"          a two-hidden-layer ReLU MLP, default loss cross-entropy,
      "modarith-decoder"    a two-layer causal transformer decoder, cross-entropy

  (the family is also readable from the model itself; it is passed so that a rule can
  carry per-family constants, as published methods do). `trainer` is a metered handle
  on the training set: `trainer.n_train`, `trainer.batch_size` (examples per driver
  step), `trainer.batch_indices` (the current step's batch), `trainer.charged`, and `trainer.loss_at(indices, params=None, loss_fn=None)`,
  which returns the differentiable training loss on the training examples `indices` --
  at the current parameters, or at `params` (a name -> tensor mapping) -- using this
  rule's `loss` or `loss_fn(outputs, targets, indices)`. Every `loss_at` call is charged
  `len(indices) / trainer.batch_size` steps against the budget.
* `UpdateRule.loss(outputs, targets, indices)` is the training loss the driver
  back-propagates each step: `outputs` are the model's outputs on the step's batch,
  `targets` the class labels and `indices` the batch's positions in the training set.
  It must return a scalar tensor. `default_loss(benchmark, outputs, targets)` is each
  benchmark's own loss. On the "mnist" benchmark the MSE loss is part of the fixed
  protocol (its grokking is a property of that objective): there the driver and
  `trainer.loss_at` always use it, and `loss` / `loss_fn` are not consulted.
* `UpdateRule.step(model, step_index)` must update `model`'s parameters **in place**
  and return nothing. `p.grad` holds the gradient of `loss` on the current batch for
  every parameter; the driver zeroes the gradients before the next backward pass.
* The step budget counts training passes: each driver step is one, and every pass made
  through `trainer.loss_at` is added. Checkpoints are taken on a fixed grid of the
  passes spent.
* The parameter *set* and every tensor shape must be unchanged at the end of the run:
  the evaluator reloads each checkpoint into a freshly built model with
  `strict=True`, so adding, removing or reshaping a parameter of `model` invalidates
  the run. Auxiliary state of your own (buffers, momenta, filters, auxiliary networks)
  may live on the rule object and is not part of the model.
* Only `torch` and the Python standard library are available. The held-out data is not
  reachable from this process.
* A step, a loss or a construction that raises invalidates the run.

baselines.docstring:
`neuralgrok` baseline: NeuralGrok, a meta-learned gradient transformation.

Zhou, Fan, Jaggi, Fu, *NeuralGrok: Accelerate Grokking by Neural Gradient
Transformation* (arXiv:2504.17243). Ported from `Blackzxy/NeuralOptGrok@a7490be`
(branch `neuralgrad`): `src/model.py::NeuralAmplifier`, `src/train.py::train`,
`transform_grads`, `trans_module_weights`, `amp_update`, and the paper's 2-layer-decoder
command (`script/neuralgrok/task1.sh`: `--lr 1e-3 --weight_decay 1e-3
--neural_hidden_dims 128,128 --inner_loop_steps 4`).
* An amplifier MLP (1 -> 128 -> 128 -> 1, ReLU, softmax over the entries of each
  parameter tensor) maps each gradient g to c * p(g) * g / ||p(g) * g|| with c = 0.2
  (`NeuralAmplifier` default); the base step then clips the total norm to 1.0 and takes
  Adam(lr 1e-3, weight decay 1e-3, betas (0.9, 0.98)) with the 10-update warm-up.
* The base model trains on D_inner only; D_outer is 1 % of the full dataset at a 50 %
  training split (`get_dataloader(p_train=0.5, p_outer=0.01)`), i.e. 2 % of the training
  set, drawn once with a fixed generator.
* Every 4 steps (`inner_loop_steps`): at the updated parameters, recompute the gradient on
  the step's inner batch, form the simulated update theta' = theta - 1e-3 * amp(g), and
  update the amplifier with Adam(lr 1e-4, weight decay 1e-3, betas (0.9, 0.98)) on the
  D_outer loss at theta' (functional evaluation; `trans_module_weights` swaps the same
  tensors into a model copy). Both extra passes go through the metered trainer.
Deviations: the paper runs only the decoder benchmark; the same constants are used on
the other families, with each family's own loss. On mini-batch families the step's batch
is drawn from the whole training set and the D_outer members are masked out of it (the
paper draws its batches from D_inner); on the MNIST family, whose MSE loss is fixed by
the protocol, the base step trains on the whole batch (D_outer included) and only the
amplifier's simulated step uses D_inner.

Zhou, Fan, Jaggi, Fu, *NeuralGrok: Accelerate Grokking by Neural Gradient
Transformation* (arXiv:2504.17243). Ported from `Blackzxy/NeuralOptGrok@a7490be`

is drawn from the whole training set and the D_outer members are masked out of it (the
paper draws its batches from D_inner); on the MNIST family, whose MSE loss is fixed by
the protocol, the base step trains on the whole batch (D_outer included) and only the
amplifier's simulated step uses D_inner.
"""

_FILE = "Omnigrok/custom_rule.py"

_CONTENT = '''class UpdateRule:
    """NeuralGrok: amplifier-transformed gradients, amplifier meta-trained on D_outer."""

    C_NORM, HIDDEN, T, LR, META_LR, WD = 0.2, (128, 128), 4, 1e-3, 1e-4, 1e-3

    def __init__(self, model, setting, budget, benchmark, trainer):
        self.benchmark = benchmark
        self.trainer = trainer
        ref = next(model.parameters())
        n = trainer.n_train
        gen = torch.Generator().manual_seed(0)
        perm = torch.randperm(n, generator=gen)
        n_outer = max(1, int(0.02 * n))
        self.outer_idx = perm[:n_outer].to(ref.device)
        self.is_outer = torch.zeros(n, dtype=torch.bool, device=ref.device)
        self.is_outer[self.outer_idx] = True
        layers, prev = [], 1
        for h in self.HIDDEN:
            layers += [torch.nn.Linear(prev, h), torch.nn.ReLU()]
            prev = h
        layers += [torch.nn.Linear(prev, 1), torch.nn.Softmax(dim=0)]
        self.amp_net = torch.nn.Sequential(*layers).to(device=ref.device, dtype=ref.dtype)
        self.opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=self.LR, weight_decay=self.WD,
                                    betas=(0.9, 0.98))
        self.sched = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.LambdaLR(
            self.opt, lambda update: 1 if update > 10 else update / 10)
        self.meta = torch.optim.Adam(self.amp_net.parameters(), lr=self.META_LR,
                                     weight_decay=self.WD, betas=(0.9, 0.98))
        self.it = 0

    def amp(self, g):
        p = self.amp_net(g)
        return self.C_NORM * p * g / torch.norm(p * g)

    def base_loss(self, outputs, targets, indices):
        return default_loss(self.benchmark, outputs, targets)

    def loss(self, outputs, targets, indices):
        keep = ~self.is_outer[indices]
        return default_loss(self.benchmark, outputs[keep], targets[keep])

    def step(self, model, step_index):
        self.it += 1
        with torch.no_grad():
            for p in model.parameters():
                p.grad = self.amp(p.grad.view(-1, 1)).view(p.shape)
        torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), max_norm=1.0)
        self.opt.step()
        self.sched.step()
        if self.it % self.T == 0:
            names = [n for n, _ in model.named_parameters()]
            params = [p for _, p in model.named_parameters()]
            inner = self.trainer.batch_indices
            inner = inner[~self.is_outer[inner]]
            loss_cp = self.trainer.loss_at(inner, loss_fn=self.base_loss)
            grads = torch.autograd.grad(loss_cp, params)
            new = {n: p.detach() - self.LR * self.amp(g.detach().reshape(-1, 1)).view(p.shape)
                   for n, p, g in zip(names, params, grads)}
            outer = self.trainer.loss_at(self.outer_idx, params=new, loss_fn=self.base_loss)
            self.meta.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
            outer.backward()
            self.meta.step()
'''
